overview: This file consists of Department of State filing-index sheets—one continuation sheet appearing twice—cataloguing reports and correspondence from 1932 through 1939 on cotton manufacturing in Japan. The indexed papers concern the general condition and outlook of the Japanese cotton industry; Commerce Department attempts to investigate artificial cotton or “staple fiber” made from wood fibre; difficulties caused by trade secrecy and unreliable production data; the acquisition and technical examination of textile samples; a historical brochure on cotton in Japan; and visits or studies by American textile-industry representatives. Several entries direct researchers to related decimal-file numbers rather than describing documents held here in full.

subfiles.title: Continuation sheet listing McConaughy’s Japan cotton outlook report
subfiles.about: A continuation filing-index sheet records the Agriculture Department’s commendation of Consul Walter P. McConaughy’s September 14 report on Japan’s cotton situation.
subfiles.summary: The sheet contains entry 12 in the file’s list of papers. It notes that the Agriculture Department found McConaughy’s report, “Japan Cotton Situation—Review and Outlook,” especially helpful in preparing its annual outlook statement; the same continuation sheet reappears on page 3.

subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Cotton Manufacture in Japan
subfiles.about: A two-sheet index describes twelve papers and cross-references concerning Japan’s cotton industry between 1932 and 1939.
subfiles.summary: The index begins with a 1932 telegram on Japan’s cotton situation and then follows Commerce Department and Kobe Consulate efforts to investigate artificial cotton or staple fiber manufactured from wood fibre. It records obstacles arising from trade secrecy, attempts to secure samples, and referral of a sample to the Bureau of Standards to determine how it differed from ordinary rayon. Later entries cover a historical brochure, an American textile-industry delegation, information on American cotton in Japan, and detailed Osaka reports, including McConaughy’s September 1939 review and the Agriculture Department’s commendation of it.

interest: The index is useful for reconstructing a dispersed documentary trail across State, Commerce, and Agriculture Department records, including explicit cross-references to other decimal-file numbers. It shows American officials trying to penetrate Japanese industrial secrecy during the early commercialization of wood-based staple fiber and seeking physical samples for scientific comparison with rayon. The entries also reveal the importance of consular reporting from Kobe and Osaka and identify contemporary reports and brochures that may survive elsewhere even though their texts are not included here. The duplication of the continuation sheet is itself evidence of the file’s administrative and microfilming history.
